title: Angles are turns
interaction: Turn a dial and a robot on the floor turns with it, its turn drawn as a pie slice that grows toward a full circle. Walk the robot around a triangle, a square and a star, pressing 'turn' at each corner: the slices stack on one pie and always close it exactly once. Then change how many steps a full turn is cut into (100, 360, 12) and watch which simple fractions of a turn (a half, a third, a quarter, a fifth) land on whole steps.
takeaway: An angle is an amount of turn, walking round any shape turns you exactly one full circle, and 360 steps per turn lands halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths on whole numbers where 100 does not.
pitfall: The size of an angle has nothing to do with the length of its arms; draw the pie at a fixed radius so a wide angle on short arms is seen to equal the same angle on long ones.
why: England KS2 maths, Year 5: 'angles at a point and 1 whole turn (total 360°)', and drawing and measuring angles in degrees. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-mathematics-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-mathematics-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: unit-circle (level 1) measures angles in degrees and radians and reads off sine and cosine; this page has only turns and pie slices, no coordinates, and is the step before it.
needsSource: none

title: Area & volume: covering and filling
interaction: Drag the corner of a floor and unit tiles flood it, counted as rows of columns; stretch it long and thin and the tile count changes while the fence around it may not. Drag the corner of a box and unit cubes fill it layer by layer, counted as you go. Then press 'double it' on a toy animal: its skin needs four times the tiles and its insides eight times the cubes.
takeaway: Area is a count of squares and volume a count of cubes, so doubling a shape's size needs four times the tiles for its skin and eight times the cubes for its insides.
pitfall: Perimeter and area are different things: shapes with the same fence can have very different floors. And 'twice as big' is ambiguous: say which (edge, skin or insides) doubles.
why: England KS2 maths, Year 4: 'find the area of rectilinear shapes by counting squares'; Year 6: 'calculate, estimate and compare volume of cubes and cuboids'; PhET's Area Builder sim. https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/area-builder
overlapWith: linear-transformations (level 2) shows the determinant scaling areas; this page counts tiles and cubes directly and shows the square-cube pattern on a toy, with no matrices.
needsSource: none

title: Coin flips & streaks
interaction: Flip a coin ten times and the flips line up as a row of heads and tails with a counter for the share of heads. Keep flipping to a hundred, then a thousand: the share settles toward a half while the longest streak keeps growing and the gap between the heads count and the tails count does not shrink. Then write a 'random' row of a hundred flips yourself and let the page compare your longest streak with the coin's.
takeaway: A fair coin's share of heads settles near a half as the flips pile up, yet long streaks keep appearing, and the next flip is not pulled toward tails to even things out.
pitfall: The gambler's fallacy: after five heads the next flip is not 'due' tails. And what evens out is the share of heads, not the heads-minus-tails count, which keeps wandering; do not draw the count converging.
why: Common Core 7.SP.C.6: 'Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency'. https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/7/SP/
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem (level 2) draws the distribution of averages; this page follows one running sequence of flips, and unlike two-dice (this batch), which counts the ways an outcome can happen, it is about the long-run share and the streaks a fair coin produces.
needsSource: none

title: Counting wheels: place value & carrying
interaction: Turn the right-hand wheel of a car's distance counter one click at a time; at 9 it rolls to 0 and nudges the wheel to its left, and a carry can ripple across every wheel at once. Change how many symbols each wheel carries: with only 0 and 1 the same pile of beans needs a longer row of wheels, and with 60 the counter is a clock. Then add two numbers the way Pascal's machine did, by turning each wheel on by the second number's digit and letting the carries do the rest.
takeaway: A counter needs only a few symbols on each wheel plus a carry to the next, and changing how many symbols a wheel holds changes the writing of a count, not the count.
pitfall: Binary is not 'a different kind of number': the same beans are counted either way. And the carry is one click of the next wheel, not a 'borrowed' digit; keep the mechanism visible.
why: Common Core 4.NBT.A.1: 'a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right'; the adding mechanism is Pascal's calculator (Wikipedia). https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/4/NBT/
overlapWith: binary (level 1) toggles bits and reads them under several conventions; this page has no conventions, only wheels that carry, and binary is just the two-symbol setting of the same counter.
needsSource: none

title: Estimating: count a little, multiply
interaction: A jar fills with sweets, each dropped into a real pile, far too many to count. Drag a small window over the jar, count the sweets inside it, and multiply by how many windows cover the jar; the page then reveals the true count and how close you came. Make the window bigger or move it to a sparse corner and watch the guess get better or worse, then try the same trick on a stadium crowd.
takeaway: Counting a small patch and multiplying gets close to the real total, closer with a bigger patch from a typical spot, and never exactly right.
pitfall: A patch from the densest or the emptiest corner gives a bad estimate; the page must let the reader pick a bad patch and see it, not choose the patch for them.
why: PhET's Estimation sim (CC BY), listed in PhET's elementary school guide. https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/estimation
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem (level 2) samples formally; this page is the everyday version: one patch, one multiplication, and a comparison with the true count the page knows.

title: Fractions: fair shares
interaction: Slide to cut a chocolate bar into equal pieces and take some: the piece count and the fraction read together. Drag one bar over another to see that one half and three sixths cover exactly the same chocolate, and that a bar cut into more pieces has smaller pieces. Then share three bars among four friends and watch every friend end up with the same pile.
takeaway: A fraction is a count of equal pieces, so cutting into more pieces makes each piece smaller, and different fractions can cover exactly the same amount.
pitfall: 'Bigger bottom number, bigger fraction' is the classic error; and pieces must be equal: a bar cut unevenly into three is not thirds.

title: Growing patterns & doubling

Switch to a rule that doubles (a grain of rice on the first chessboard square, two on the next) and press the same twenty steps: the chart leaves the screen and the counter needs a wider box every few presses. Fold a sheet of paper in half, and again, and watch the layer count race the staircase.
takeaway: A pattern that adds the same each time climbs in a straight line, while one that doubles explodes past anything countable within a few dozen steps.

title: The infinite hotel
interaction: A hotel with rooms numbered 1, 2, 3 and on past the edge of the screen is full. Pick a rule for the guests ('everyone move up one', 'everyone move to double your number') and the page applies it to every room you can scroll to: a free room appears, or endlessly many do, and no two guests ever share. Then pair the whole numbers off against the even numbers, and against the fractions laid out in a grid, and scroll as far as you like looking for one left out.
takeaway: A hotel with no last room can always take more guests, and the whole numbers can be paired off one-to-one with just the even ones, which no finite row of rooms can do.

title: Mirrors & turns: symmetry
interaction: Draw on one side of a mirror line and the page draws the reflection on the other; drag the line to tilt it and the reflection follows. Swap the mirror for a turntable and set how many copies go around the centre to make a snowflake or a pinwheel. Drop in letters and shapes and the page tries every flip and turn, counting the ones that land the shape exactly on itself.
takeaway: A shape is symmetric when a flip or a turn lands it exactly on itself, and the count shows that some shapes have several such moves and some have none.
pitfall: A shape can have turn symmetry with no mirror line (an S, a pinwheel), and a rectangle's diagonal is not a mirror line; show both, since both are common wrong answers.

title: Per cent: out of a hundred
interaction: A price tag and a hundred-square sit side by side; turn the discount dial and squares grey out as the price falls, the same number of squares whatever the price. Then set two different prices and apply the same per cent: the bars lose different amounts. Finally take 50% off and then add 50% back and watch the bar fail to return to where it started.
takeaway: Per cent counts out of a hundred of whatever you start with, so the same per cent takes a bigger bite from a bigger price, and a cut and a matching rise do not cancel.
pitfall: A 50% drop followed by a 50% rise is not a return to the start, and '20% off then 10% off' is not 30% off; show both rather than treating per cents as plain numbers that add.

title: Rectangles & primes

takeaway: Some counts of chairs can be set out as a rectangle in several ways and some only as a single line, and those single-line counts, the primes, are scattered across the hundred-square with no even spacing.

title: Rolling a wheel: pi
interaction: Drag a wheel along a ruler and a paint mark on its rim leaves a dot each time it comes round; the gap between dots is a bit more than three wheel-widths. Then slice a circle into wedges, set how many, and drag them into a row that gets closer and closer to a rectangle as the count goes up.
takeaway: Every wheel rolls out a little more than three of its widths per turn, whatever its size, and the same number appears when the circle's wedges are laid out as a near-rectangle.

title: Scaling a recipe
interaction: A pancake recipe for four sits beside a dial for the number of eaters; turn it and every ingredient's bar grows or shrinks together, with the counts read off. Then mix orange squash: add cups of concentrate and the glass darkens, add cups of water and it pales, and two glasses with the same ratio come out the same colour whatever their size. Add one cup of each to both glasses and watch their colours split apart.
takeaway: Scaling a recipe multiplies every ingredient by the same number, and the colour of the squash depends on the ratio of concentrate to water, not on how much is in the glass.
pitfall: Adding the same amount to both parts is not scaling: the page must show the additive error (one more cup of each) changing the colour, since that is the most common ratio mistake.

title: Shapes that tile a floor
interaction: Pick a shape from the tray (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) and tap a corner: the page fits copies of the shape around that corner one at a time until it closes the turn, leaves a gap or overlaps. A shape that closes the turn exactly floods the floor with copies; one that does not leaves holes. Then take a square tile and bend one edge: the opposite edge bends to match and the floor still fills, Escher-style.
takeaway: A shape tiles a floor when its corners fit together into exactly one full turn, which triangles, squares and hexagons do and regular pentagons and octagons do not.
pitfall: Regular pentagons do not tile, but some irregular pentagons do (fifteen kinds are known), so the page must say 'this pentagon', never 'pentagons'.

title: Speed: how far each second
interaction: Set one runner's speed as paces per second and press go: a clock ticks, the runner moves, and a line climbs on a distance-time chart, one point per tick. Add a second runner with a different speed and the two lines show who is ahead at any tick and where they cross. Make a runner stop to tie a shoelace and watch the line go flat, then put the tortoise and the hare on the track.
takeaway: Speed is how far you get in each tick of the clock, which on a distance-time chart is the steepness of the line: steeper is faster, flat is standing still.
pitfall: Height on the chart is distance, not speed: a runner who is ahead is not necessarily faster; and the hare's rest is a flat stretch, not a dip (the line only goes down if the runner turns back).

title: Sunflower spirals
interaction: A flower head grows one seed at a time, each placed a fixed turn after the last and pushed outward; a dial sets that turn. At a quarter turn or a third the seeds line up in spokes with wasted gaps; near the 'golden' turn, a bit more than a third, the head fills evenly and families of spirals appear. Tap a spiral and the page counts the spirals running each way (21 and 34, say), then count them yourself on a photograph of a real sunflower.

title: Two dice
interaction: Pick the total you would bet on, then roll two dice; each roll adds a block to its total's column. Roll ten at a time, then a hundred, and the columns grow into the same triangle every time, with 7 on top. Flip the board over to see the 36 ways two dice can land, coloured by total, and count the ways to make 7 against the ways to make 2.

title: What an average hides
interaction: Ten friends' weekly pocket money sits as coin stacks on a plank; drag any stack along it and the plank tips until a pointer finds the one place it balances, the mean, while a second marker stands at the middle stack, the median. Drag one friend's stack far to the right (a generous uncle) and watch the balance point slide after it while the middle marker barely moves. Then compare two classes with the same balance point but very different spreads.
takeaway: The mean is where the data balances, so one far-off value drags it along, while the median stays with the middle of the crowd.
pitfall: 'Average' does not mean 'typical' or 'most': with one big outlier most people are below the mean, and the tallest bar of a chart (the mode) is a third thing again.

title: Information theory & channel capacity

title: Stopping a car: twice the speed, four times the skid

title: Tap to pay

title: What a camera's sensor counts
interaction: Open the shutter on a drawn camera pointed at a scene and watch light arrive as specks landing in a grid of tiny buckets, each bucket counting its specks; the picture forms from the counts, and a slider sets how long the shutter stays open. title: Falling & parachutes

Pump the air out of the chamber and drop them again: they land together, as on the Moon. title: Friction & grip

title: Helicopters: a spinning wing
interaction: Spin up a helicopter's rotor and lift off: the blades are wings going round, and the faster they spin or the more they tilt, the harder they throw air down and the more the helicopter is pushed up. Tilt the whole rotor disc to slide forward, backward or sideways; then switch off the tail rotor and watch the body spin the opposite way to the blades, and turn it back on to point where you like.

interaction: Flick a top with a chosen spin and watch it stand; tip it with a nudge and instead of falling over it leans and slowly wobbles round in a circle. As friction slows the spin the wobble widens and quickens, until the top finally topples. Try a gyroscope held by one end and a bicycle wheel held by its axle, run by the same equations.
takeaway: A spinning thing resists being tipped: a push on it turns into a slow sideways wobble, and it falls over only once the spin runs down.
pitfall: Spinning does not make the top lighter or cancel gravity; gravity pulls on it the whole time, and the top answers by wobbling round instead of falling.

Ciechanowski's 'Bicycle' explainer is verified in his archive listing https://ciechanow.ski/bicycle/ (content not checked this session).

title: Springs & spring scales
interaction: Hang weights on a spring one at a time and watch it stretch the same extra amount for each one, so a ruler beside it becomes a scale; swap in a stiffer spring, or put two springs side by side or end to end, and compare how far they stretch for the same weights. Load it past its limit and see it stay stretched when the weights come off; then press a bathroom scale, a mattress and a pogo stick and watch the same rule at work.
takeaway: A spring stretches by the same extra amount for each extra weight, which is what makes it a scale, until it is pulled past the point where it stops coming back.
pitfall: A spring does not push back with the same force however far it is stretched, and one stretched past its limit is not broken but bent: it still works, from a new rest length.
why: PhET 'Hooke's Law' is the standard primary and middle-school simulation of springs (https://www.compadre.org/Precollege/items/similar.cfm?ID=14156); KS2 Year 5 forces collections add springs to levers, pulleys and gears (https://stem.org.uk/node/12033).
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page sets a spring bouncing and plots its response; this page never lets it move: it is the stretch per weight that makes a scale, and the limit beyond which it stays bent.

title: Submarines: sinking and rising on purpose
interaction: Flood a submarine's tanks with sea water and it grows heavier than the water it pushes aside and sinks; blow the water out with compressed air and it rises; let in just enough and it hovers, neither rising nor sinking. Tilt the fins and drive forward to glide up or down; a pair of scales shows the submarine's weight against the weight of water it displaces at every moment. Hover, then add a small extra load and watch what happens.
takeaway: A submarine goes down and up by changing its own weight with water taken in or pushed out, until it weighs just as much as the water it displaces.
pitfall: A submarine does not sink because it is made of steel: full of air it floats like a ship, and it only sinks when water replaces the air. Hovering is a knife edge: a little too heavy and it keeps sinking, which is why submarines trim constantly.
why: PhET 'Buoyancy: Basics', in PhET's middle-school simulation list, https://phet.colorado.edu/en/simulations/buoyancy-basics ('how do submarines sink and float' is a common search question)
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page balances forces on carts; here the two forces are the submarine's weight and the water's upward push, and the reader changes one of them. Floating itself is not in the catalogue; this is the one vehicle that floats, sinks and hovers by choice.

title: Pumping a swing with nobody pushing

A trace shows each swing's height over time; a second rider pumps seated by leaning back and forward instead. Shorten the chains and feel the timing change.

title: Temperature & what the hand feels
interaction: Touch things around a room (a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a wool hat, a tiled floor) with a hand that feels how fast heat leaves it, then with a thermometer that reads its own temperature once it has settled: the thermometer says they are all the same, the hand says the metal is colder. Put the thermometer in a kettle and watch its liquid climb as its particles jiggle harder. Pour a cup of boiling water into a bath of warm water and see which temperature wins.
takeaway: Things that have sat in the same room are all at the same temperature; what the hand feels is how fast heat flows out of it, which is why metal feels colder than wood.

title: Thermos flasks & keeping things warm

title: How a touchscreen feels your finger
interaction: Drag a finger over a screen whose glass is made see-through: under it is a grid of thin crossing wires, and at every crossing a small store of charge that your finger, a bag of salty water, draws a little from when it comes near. The grid lights up where the draw is biggest and the phone marks the spot between the brightest crossings. Press harder and nothing changes; put on a woollen glove and the glow fades to nothing; add a second finger and a second spot appears; drip water on the glass and a false spot wanders.
takeaway: A touchscreen does not feel pressure: it notices where your body draws a little charge from a grid of crossings under the glass, which is why gloves and water confuse it and pressing harder does nothing.
needsSource: none; mutual capacitance at each crossing reduced in proportion to the overlap with a conductive footprint, then a centroid between the strongest crossings.
pitfall: No pressure and no warmth is sensed (older resistive screens did sense pressure; say so). The finger does not conduct electricity into the phone; it only needs to be near. A plastic stylus does nothing, and a touchscreen stylus works because its tip is conductive.
why: 'Touchscreen' averaged about 12,200 views a month on English Wikipedia in 2025 (https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Touchscreen/monthly/2025010100/2025123100).

title: Train wheels: why trains stay on the rails
interaction: Roll a pair of train wheels joined by an axle along two rails and nudge it sideways: because each wheel is a slight cone, the side pushed outward rides on a bigger circle and runs faster, and the pair swings back to the middle, wobbling less and less. Swap in flat wheels and the pair drifts to the rail's edge and leans on its flange; make the cone steeper and the wobble gets wilder. Send the pair round a curve and watch it steer itself with no differential.
takeaway: A train steers itself because its wheels are cones: whichever side rides up onto the bigger part of the cone turns the axle back toward the middle.
pitfall: The flanges do not steer the train: on straight track they rarely touch the rail, and a train running on its flanges squeals and wears. The wheels are not free to spin separately as a car's are; they are fixed to one axle, which is why the cone is needed.
why: Feynman's explanation of conical train wheels, retold in Tadashi Tokieda's widely shared video, https://kottke.org/21/10/the-simple-physics-trick-that-helps-trains-stay-on-their-tracks
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page is a mass on a spring and a pendulum; the wheelset's wobble is a geometric oscillation on rails with no spring at all, and the page is about steering, not resonance.

title: Vibrations & sound
interaction: Twang a ruler held over the edge of a table: the strip wobbles, and a row of air particles passes the push along to an ear, each one jiggling in place while the squeeze travels down the row; the speakers play the note. Slide the ruler in to shorten it and the wobble quickens and the note rises; twang it harder and the wobble widens and the note gets louder. Move the ear away and the sound fades, then pump the air out of a jar around a ringing bell and nothing arrives at all.

title: Water pressure & hydraulics
interaction: Punch holes at different heights in a tall bottle and the jets reach different distances, the lowest furthest. Lower a gauge into a lake, then into a thin tube of the same depth: it reads the same, deeper means harder, however wide or narrow the water. Push down on the small piston of a hydraulic lift and the big piston raises a car with a far bigger push, but rises a far shorter way; try the same with a bicycle brake and a digger's arm.
takeaway: Water pushes harder the deeper you go, whatever the shape of the container, and a liquid passes a push along so that a small push on a small piston becomes a big push on a big one that moves less far.

title: Why metal feels cold
interaction: A table with a metal spoon, a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a woollen glove, all at room temperature, with a thermometer that reads the same on each. Drag a finger onto any one: a strip of heat colour flows out of the fingertip into the object, fast into the metal and barely at all into the wool, and a 'feels like' dial follows the fingertip's own temperature. One control: the room temperature; set the room hot and the same metal now feels hottest. The flow is a heat-conduction model with each material's real conductivity.
takeaway: Everything on the table is the same temperature; the metal feels cold because it carries heat out of your finger fastest, and the same metal feels hottest in a hot room.
needs: Thermal conductivity, density and heat capacity of a few common materials (a metal, wood, plastic, wool, skin), from textbook or Wikipedia tables (CC BY-SA); under ten constants.
needsSource: Under ten published material constants (textbook tables; Wikipedia CC BY-SA); facts, no dataset
pitfall: Metal is not colder than wood, and cold does not flow into your hand: heat flows out of it, and a thermometer shows the two objects equal.
why: Veritasium, 'Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood If They're the Same Temperature?' (a classic misconception video): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vqDbMEdLiCs; England KS2 Year 5 lists thermal conductivity among material properties.
overlapWith: entropy: that page shows heat flowing between fast and slow particles at level 2; here it is one finger on one object, and the only question is how fast heat leaves the skin.

title: Chromatography: separating by stickiness
interaction: Inject a mixture at the top of a column and watch each molecule hop at random between the moving phase and the stationary phase, with the time spent stuck set by its partition coefficient, so the bands separate and broaden; a detector at the end draws the chromatogram. Slide the flow rate and the plate height traces the van Deemter curve with its minimum, as eddy paths, diffusion along the column and slow exchange each take their turn at blurring the bands; lengthen the column or change the packing to improve the resolution.
takeaway: A column separates molecules by how much of the time each spends stuck rather than moving, and there is a best flow speed: slower and diffusion blurs the bands, faster and the molecules cannot keep up with the exchange.
pitfall: Most chromatography is not a sieve by size: two molecules of the same size separate by how differently they stick, and the bands are Gaussian because the hopping is random.
why: Undergraduate analytical chemistry teaches band broadening through the van Deemter equation (Bates College chromatography learning objectives): https://www.bates.edu/chemistry-biochemistry/files/2012/01/wenzel-chrom-learning-objectives.pdf
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: that page shows why sums of random steps are Gaussian; this one uses that fact to separate molecules and to find the flow rate that separates them best.
needsSource: none

title: Colloids: why particles stay apart, and when they stick
interaction: Run charged particles in water that diffuse and interact through the DLVO potential, a short-range van der Waals attraction plus a repulsion from the ion cloud around each particle, drawn as a curve beside the box. Slide the salt concentration and watch the cloud shrink, the barrier in the curve sink and the particles flocculate; raise the surface charge to re-stabilize them, and compare the critical salt concentration for mono-, di- and trivalent ions.
takeaway: Particles in water stay apart because of a cloud of ions around each one, and adding salt shrinks that cloud until they stick, which is why a river drops its mud where it meets the sea.
pitfall: A colloid is not stable because its particles float: they are denser than water and would settle quickly once clumped, and it is the repulsion between them, not Brownian motion alone, that keeps them apart.
why: TU/e 'Polymer and colloid science' covers electrical double layers, van der Waals forces and DLVO theory: https://eduxchange.nl/ewuu/guest/catalog-tue/courses/polymer-and-colloid-science_df728589-acde-471e-927b-089f5e54e90d
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page is a one-component box; this one models suspended particles whose fate depends on the ions around them.
needsSource: none

title: Choosing a material: composites & Ashby charts
interaction: Pan and zoom a chart of stiffness against density for hundreds of real materials and drag the selection line for a light, stiff beam or a light, strong tie to see which materials rise to the top. Mix a fibre and a matrix with a volume-fraction slider and the composite appears between them on the chart, bounded by the rule-of-mixtures lines for aligned and transverse fibres; a fibre pull-out panel shows why a composite tolerates cracks that would shatter its ceramic fibres alone.
takeaway: No material is best on its own: which one wins depends on the job's combination of properties, and a composite earns a spot on the chart that neither of its parts could reach.
needs: Elastic moduli and densities for crystalline materials from an open database, plus a small table for polymers, woods and composites.
pitfall: Stiffness and strength are different properties, carbon fibre is stiff where aramid is strong, and a composite's stiffness along its fibres says nothing about the direction across them.
why: MIT OCW 3.22 Mechanical Behavior of Materials treats elastic and plastic behaviour across metals, ceramics and polymers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-22-mechanical-behavior-of-materials-spring-2008/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page compares shapes for one material budget; this one compares materials for one shape and shows how a composite gets around the trade-off.
needsSource: Materials Project (CC BY 4.0) for computed bulk and shear moduli and densities of crystalline materials; polymers, woods and composites are absent there and need a hand-made table of published values (Ashby/CES data is proprietary), which is a weakness of this page.

title: Corrosion: why iron rusts and zinc saves it
interaction: Drag a point over the potential-pH map of iron in water, computed live from the Nernst lines of its species, and see which form is stable there: bare metal, dissolved ions or a protective oxide. Couple the iron to a second metal (zinc, copper, tin) and the mixed-potential diagram shows where the two electrode curves cross and which metal dissolves; change the oxygen level, pH or salt content and watch the corrosion current move.
takeaway: Whether a metal corrodes depends on pH and potential together, and sacrificial zinc protects steel by pulling its potential into the region where iron stays metal.
needs: Standard potentials and free energies of formation for the iron, zinc, copper and tin species in water, and exchange current densities for the mixed-potential diagram.
pitfall: Rusting is not iron simply reacting with air: it is an electrochemical cell with anodic and cathodic spots on the same piece of metal, which is why salt water speeds it up so much.
why: MIT OCW 10.626 Lecture 2 builds cell thermodynamics from the Nernst equation, the basis of Pourbaix and Evans diagrams: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/chemical-engineering/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/lecture-notes/MIT10_626S14_Lec2.pdf
overlapWith: electrode-kinetics (proposed): that page holds one electrode under control; this one lets two reactions on the same metal find their own potential and maps the outcome over pH.
needsSource: ΔG°f and standard potentials from the NBS tables of chemical thermodynamic properties (Wagman et al. 1982, a US-government compilation; confirm redistribution terms) or equivalent NIST data; exchange current densities from the literature. The Pourbaix Atlas itself is copyrighted and not needed: the lines are computed.

title: Diffusion in solids
interaction: Watch atoms in a lattice hop into neighbouring vacancies at a rate set by temperature and an activation energy, and plot the concentration profile of carbon diffusing into iron against the erf solution of Fick's law; the depth grows with the square root of time, and a temperature slider changes the rate by orders of magnitude. Join two metals with different hop rates and watch the interface markers drift (the Kirkendall effect) while vacancies pile up on the faster side.
takeaway: Atoms in a solid move by hopping into empty sites, so diffusion depth grows as the square root of time and rises exponentially with temperature: a treatment that takes an hour at 900 °C would take centuries at room temperature.
needs: The diffusion prefactor and activation energy for carbon in iron.
pitfall: Nothing pushes the atoms toward low concentration; each hops at random, and the net flow from high to low comes only from there being more atoms on one side.
why: MIT OCW 3.205 covers Fick's laws, self- and interdiffusion and the Kirkendall effect: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-205-thermodynamics-and-kinetics-of-materials-fall-2006/pages/calendar
overlapWith: entropy: that page mixes gases by removing a wall; this one is diffusion through a solid lattice via vacancies, with its Arrhenius rate and its uses in steel and chips.
needsSource: Published D0 and Q for carbon in iron (textbook numbers).

title: Dislocations: why metals bend and alloys resist
interaction: Shear a two-dimensional crystal of simulated atoms with an edge dislocation inside it and watch the defect glide one row of bonds at a time at a stress far below what sliding the whole plane would take; remove the dislocation and the perfect crystal holds until it fails all at once. Sprinkle in larger or smaller foreign atoms and the dislocation snags on them so the crystal needs more stress to yield; keep deforming and dislocations pile up and the metal hardens.
takeaway: A metal bends at a stress a thousand times below the strength of its bonds because a dislocation moves one row of bonds at a time, and an alloy is harder because foreign atoms get in its way.
pitfall: Crystals do not deform by whole planes sliding at once; the theoretical strength computed that way is a thousand times higher than what any real metal shows.
why: MITx 3.012S.3x Structure of Materials covers dislocation descriptors and motion: https://openlearninglibrary.mit.edu/courses/course-v1:MITx+3.012S.3x+1T2019/about
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page colors members by stress; this one goes inside the metal to the defect that lets it yield and the atoms that stop it.
needsSource: none

title: Van der Waals forces: why neutral atoms stick
interaction: Place two neutral atoms, each modelled as an electron on a spring to its nucleus, and drag them closer: the page solves their coupled oscillations and shows the zero-point energy drop as their flickering dipoles fall into step, tracing an attraction that falls as the sixth power of distance. Slide the atoms' polarizability to deepen the well, add permanent dipoles and a hydrogen bond to build up the full potential curve, and compare the computed well depths with the boiling points of the noble gases and halogens.
takeaway: Even neutral atoms attract because their electron clouds flicker in step, and that attraction grows with the size of the cloud, which is why bigger molecules boil hotter.
needs: Polarizabilities and boiling points of the noble gases and halogens.
pitfall: Dispersion is not negligible: summed over a large molecule it rivals a hydrogen bond and it is the force a gecko climbs with; nor is it a weak form of the chemical bond.
why: MIT OCW 3.091 Fall 2018 syllabus runs from molecular orbitals into intermolecular forces: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/pages/syllabus/
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page takes the attraction between molecules as given; this one shows where it comes from and why its size varies.
needsSource: Polarizabilities and boiling points from the NIST Chemistry WebBook or the CRC Handbook (a short table of published numbers).

title: Electrode kinetics: Nernst to Butler-Volmer
interaction: Set the potential of an electrode in a solution of a redox couple and watch the concentration ratio at its surface follow the Nernst equation while the current follows the Butler-Volmer curve, with a Tafel plot alongside. A diffusion layer in front of the electrode is computed on a grid, so sweeping the potential up and down traces a cyclic voltammogram whose peaks grow with the sweep rate, and pushing too hard shows the current starve as molecules cannot arrive fast enough.
takeaway: The electrode potential sets the ratio of oxidized to reduced molecules at the surface, and the current is set by how far you push from that balance, until diffusion caps it.
pitfall: The Nernst equation gives a cell's voltage with no current flowing; under load the voltage is lower by the overpotentials, and current is not the speed of the electrons.
why: MIT OCW 10.626 Electrochemical Energy Systems covers the thermodynamics, reaction kinetics and transport of electrochemical cells: https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: redox-batteries: that page follows ions and electrons through a lithium cell; this one models the interface itself, how potential sets composition and current.
needsSource: none (a textbook couple such as ferri/ferrocyanide with literature rate constants)

title: Enzyme kinetics
interaction: Watch one enzyme molecule bind substrate, convert it and release product as a random sequence of events while a thousand copies beside it build the smooth rate curve; slide the substrate concentration and see the rate saturate at Vmax with Km read off at half-height. Add a competitive or a non-competitive inhibitor and watch the curve and its Lineweaver-Burk line change in different ways; load real Km and kcat values for enzymes from carbonic anhydrase to catalase.
takeaway: An enzyme's rate climbs with substrate only until every enzyme is busy, so the plateau measures the enzyme's speed and the half-way point its grip on the substrate, and an inhibitor reveals which of the two it attacks.
needs: Km and kcat values for a handful of enzymes.
pitfall: Vmax is never reached, only approached, and Km is not simply the binding constant: it also contains the catalytic rate.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 Lecture 35 (enzyme catalysis: Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Burk) and 5.07 session 4: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/5_60_lecture35
overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page follows one glucose through the pathways; this one models how fast any enzyme works and what limits it.
needsSource: BRENDA enzyme database (CC BY 4.0).

title: Cracks & fracture
interaction: Stretch a sheet made of a lattice of breakable springs and watch the stress concentrate at the tip of a notch the reader cuts; raise the load until the crack runs, and plot the breaking stress against the notch length to find Griffith's rule. Switch the material from glass-like to metal-like: springs that yield before breaking blunt the tip and absorb energy, so the same crack needs far more stress to run.
takeaway: A crack grows when the elastic energy it releases pays for the new surface it makes, so a longer crack needs less stress to run, and a material's strength is set by its flaws as much as by its bonds.
needs: Fracture toughness and modulus values for a few materials, to label the glass-like and metal-like settings.
pitfall: Strength is not a fixed material constant: Griffith's glass fibres were many times stronger than bulk glass because they had smaller flaws, and a scratch is what makes a pane weak.
why: MIT OCW 3.22 Mechanical Behavior of Materials covers fracture across metals, ceramics and polymers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-22-mechanical-behavior-of-materials-spring-2008/pages/syllabus
overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page fails members when their load limit is exceeded; this one shows why the limit depends on cracks and how a crack decides to run.
needsSource: Published K_IC and modulus values (textbook numbers); the spring network needs no data.

title: Free energy of mixing & phase diagrams
interaction: Drag the interaction energy and the temperature of a two-component regular solution and watch its free-energy curve bend; wherever a common tangent lies below the curve the page draws it and splits the mixture into two phases at the tangent points. Sweep the temperature and the phase diagram assembles underneath (miscibility gap and spinodal); add solid and liquid curves to build lens and eutectic diagrams, and drag a composition to read the lever rule.
takeaway: A phase diagram is the shadow of free-energy curves: a mixture splits wherever a straight line between two compositions lies below the curve, and the tangent points become the phase boundaries.
pitfall: A two-phase region on a phase diagram is not a phase; the mixture there is two phases of the boundary compositions, in amounts the lever rule gives.
why: MIT OCW 3.012 problem set 6 builds phase diagrams from common tangents on free-energy curves: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-012-fundamentals-of-materials-science-fall-2005/2cbcd5557e2886b8ce70445f8312394b_ps06_sol.pdf
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page tracks one substance on a pressure-temperature diagram; this one derives a two-component diagram from free energy.
needsSource: none

title: Glass: the liquid that ran out of time
interaction: Cool a box of two sizes of simulated atoms at a rate the reader chooses and watch the volume-temperature plot: cooled slowly, a pure sample snaps into a crystal with a sharp drop; cooled quickly, or mixed, it jams into a glass at a gentle kink whose temperature rises with the cooling rate. A mean-squared-displacement plot shows the atoms caging each other as the glass forms, and a structure panel compares the crystal's repeating rows with the glass's frozen liquid.
takeaway: A glass is a liquid cooled too fast to crystallize, so its atoms jam where they stand, and the temperature where that happens depends on how fast it was cooled.
pitfall: Window glass does not flow at room temperature; old panes are thicker at one edge because of how they were made, not because the glass sagged.
why: MIT OCW 3.091 Fall 2018 syllabus includes glasses after crystals and defects: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/pages/syllabus/
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page freezes a box into a crystal; this one cools a mixture fast enough that it cannot, and shows what forms instead.
needsSource: none

title: Hartree-Fock: the self-consistent field
interaction: Step through a self-consistent-field calculation on H2 or HeH+ in a minimal basis: start from a guessed orbital, build the Fock matrix from it, solve, and watch the orbitals, the electron density and the energy settle iteration by iteration until the field the electrons make is the field they were solved in. Then drag the bond length to trace the energy curve, and switch on the exact two-determinant answer in the same basis to see the mean-field curve go wrong as the bond breaks.
takeaway: Each electron is solved in the average field of the others and the loop repeats until nothing changes, which captures most of the bond but misses the correlation between electrons that matters most when a bond is pulled apart.
needs: STO-3G exponents and contraction coefficients for H and He; all integrals are computed in the browser.
pitfall: Exchange is not a force between electrons, and the Hartree-Fock energy is an upper bound: the missing correlation energy is small per electron but is exactly what a stretched bond needs.
why: MIT OCW 5.61 covers molecular orbital theory, and the Szabo & Ostlund HeH+ SCF program is the standard worked example (CCL archive): https://ccl.net/cca/software/SOURCES/FORTRAN/szabo/index.html
overlapWith: huckel-molecular-orbitals (proposed): Hückel takes the matrix elements as parameters; this page computes them from the electrons' own repulsion and iterates to self-consistency.
needsSource: STO-3G parameters from the Basis Set Exchange (MolSSI, openly licensed; confirm the current licence) or as printed in Szabo & Ostlund (a dozen numbers).

title: Molecular orbitals & conjugation
interaction: Snap carbon atoms into chains and rings to build a π system (ethene, butadiene, benzene, cyclobutadiene, a cyanine dye); the page diagonalizes the Hückel matrix and draws the molecular orbitals as signed lobes on the atoms beside an energy ladder filled with the π electrons. Lengthen a dye chain and watch the HOMO-LUMO gap shrink while a swatch shows the color it absorbs; close a chain into a ring and watch the levels regroup into the aromatic pattern, or fail to for a four-membered ring.
takeaway: Electrons delocalized over a π system fill a ladder of orbitals whose gap narrows as the system grows, which is why longer dyes are redder and why a six-membered ring is stable where a four-membered one is not.
needs: Measured absorption maxima of a cyanine dye series for the color panel, to set beside the computed gap.
pitfall: Benzene's bonds do not alternate between single and double; the orbitals spread over the whole ring, and the two Kekulé drawings are a convention, not structures it flips between.
why: MIT OCW 5.61 Physical Chemistry devotes Lecture 26 to qualitative MO theory (Hückel): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/resources/qualitative-mo-theory-huckel/
overlapWith: chemical-bonds: that page builds molecules from localized electron pairs and VSEPR shapes; this one computes delocalized orbital energies and shapes from the Hückel Hamiltonian.
needsSource: Published λmax values of the classic cyanine dye series (literature numbers, not a licensed dataset); the Hückel model itself needs no data.

title: Liquid crystals & the LCD pixel
interaction: Run a lattice of rod-like molecules (Lebwohl-Lasher Monte Carlo) and slide the temperature: above a point the rods point every way, below it they agree on a direction and the order parameter jumps. Apply a voltage across the cell and watch the rods swing toward the field; place the twisted cell between crossed polarizers and the page computes the light that gets through, so the pixel goes from bright to dark as the voltage rises.
takeaway: A liquid crystal is a liquid whose molecules agree on a direction, and a small voltage re-aims them, which turns a pixel from light to dark in front of a backlight.
pitfall: The liquid crystal in a screen emits no light; it is a voltage-controlled shutter, and the colors come from filters over a white backlight.
why: TU/e 'Polymer and colloid science' covers liquid-crystal phases and Onsager theory, and EngineerGuy's LCD teardown is a widely shared explainer: https://eduxchange.nl/ewuu/guest/catalog-tue/courses/polymer-and-colloid-science_300b6aa7-1f16-46f4-be98-05e87310000a
overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page has solid, liquid and gas; this one adds the state between liquid and crystal and the device built on it.
needsSource: none

title: Mass spectrometry
interaction: Ionize a sample and send the ions down a quadrupole whose radio-frequency and DC voltages the reader sets; the page integrates each ion's equation of motion and shows which masses ride stably to the detector and which crash into the rods, with the stability diagram beside. Scan the voltages to sweep across masses and build the spectrum; pick an element or a small molecule and its isotope pattern (chlorine's 3:1 pair, bromine's 1:1 pair) is computed from natural abundances and set beside a measured spectrum.
takeaway: A mass spectrometer sorts ions by mass-to-charge with electric fields, and only ions within a narrow window of mass ride the oscillating field stably, so sweeping the field reads out the sample one mass at a time.
needs: Isotopic abundances of the elements and a few reference spectra.
pitfall: The axis is mass-to-charge, not mass: a doubly charged ion appears at half its mass, and the tallest peak is not necessarily the molecular ion.
why: OCR A-level Chemistry A (H432) and AQA include mass spectrometry and isotope patterns: https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/chemistry/ocr/

title: NMR: spins, pulses & spectra
interaction: Put nuclear spins in a magnetic field, fire a 90° pulse and watch the net magnetization tip and precess while the detector records the decaying signal, then Fourier-transform it into a peak. Add a second spin with a scalar coupling and the peak splits into a doublet; set real chemical shifts for ethanol's three environments and watch the whole spectrum assemble, with linewidth following the decay rate.
takeaway: An NMR spectrometer listens to nuclei precessing after a pulse, and each nucleus's note is shifted by its electron surroundings and split by its neighbours, so the spectrum reads out the molecule's structure.
needs: Chemical shifts and coupling constants for a few molecules (ethanol, ethyl acetate).
pitfall: The spectrum is not scanned one frequency at a time; it is the Fourier transform of one decaying signal, and 'spin' does not mean the nucleus is physically spinning like a top.
why: OCR A-level Chemistry A (H432) module 6 includes proton and carbon-13 NMR with a chemical-shift data sheet: https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/chemistry/ocr/

title: Nucleation & crystal growth
interaction: Cool a simulated liquid below its freezing point and watch small clusters form and dissolve until one passes the critical size and grows, while a plot of the free energy of a cluster against its radius shows the hill it had to climb; deepen the undercooling and the hill shrinks, more nuclei survive and the solid ends up as many small grains instead of a few large ones. Then run a phase-field model of a solidifying front on a grid and watch it break into dendrites whose arms thin as the undercooling rises.
takeaway: A liquid below its freezing point does not freeze at once: a solid seed must first grow past a critical size against its own surface, so deeper undercooling means more seeds and finer grains, and a growing front splits into branches.
pitfall: Freezing does not start everywhere at once when the freezing point is reached; pure water can be cooled well below 0 °C, and snowflakes branch because the front is unstable, not because the molecules know a shape.
why: MIT OCW 3.205's calendar runs from diffusion to nucleation, solidification, spinodal decomposition and coarsening: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-205-thermodynamics-and-kinetics-of-materials-fall-2006/pages/calendar

title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence & photochemistry
interaction: Shine a light pulse on a population of molecules shown on a Jablonski ladder and watch them climb and then leave the excited state by competing routes (fluorescence, internal conversion, intersystem crossing, phosphorescence), each with a rate constant on a slider. A plot of emitted light against time shows the lifetime and quantum yield; switch the lamp off to see the slow phosphorescent tail, and add a quencher to watch the Stern-Volmer line steepen.

title: Quantum dots: color from size
interaction: Slide the radius of a semiconductor nanocrystal from 2 to 10 nm and the page solves the confinement energy of its electron and hole, adds the bulk band gap and shows the color it emits, next to a ladder of discrete levels that spreads as the dot shrinks. Switch the material and compare the computed emission with measured peak wavelengths of real dots; a density-of-states panel shows the smooth bulk band breaking into sharp levels as the box closes in.
takeaway: Trap an electron in a box a few nanometres wide and the energy it gives back as light is set by the size of the box, so one material glows in every color depending on how small it is made.

title: Free energy & the equilibrium constant
interaction: Drag the extent of a reaction (N2O4 ⇌ 2 NO2, with real enthalpy and entropy) along a plot of the mixture's Gibbs energy and watch it fall to a minimum part-way, where the composition matches the equilibrium constant; switch off the mixing-entropy term that bends the curve to see why the reaction would otherwise run to completion. Change the temperature and the pressure and watch the minimum, K and the yield move.
takeaway: A reaction runs downhill in free energy and stops at the bottom of a curve that lies at a mixture rather than at completion, because mixing itself lowers the free energy; the depth of that bottom is the equilibrium constant.
needs: Standard enthalpies of formation and entropies for N2O4 and NO2.
pitfall: A negative ΔG° does not mean the reaction goes to completion and a positive one does not mean it does not happen; the sign sets K, and the mixture always settles at a minimum between the two extremes.
why: MIT OCW 5.60 Thermodynamics & Kinetics covers chemical equilibrium of gas- and solution-phase reactions through the Gibbs energy: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008
overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page reaches equilibrium kinetically, as equal forward and reverse rates; this one locates it thermodynamically as the minimum of G and ties it to K and temperature.
needsSource: NIST-JANAF thermochemical tables (NIST Standard Reference Data, free to use with citation; a few numbers).

title: Rubber & polymer chains: the entropic spring
interaction: Grab the ends of a freely-jointed chain of a few hundred links and pull; the page samples the chain's random walks and shows the count of shapes that fit each end-to-end distance collapsing, with the restoring force computed from that count and the temperature. Turn up the temperature and the stretched chain pulls harder and shortens; cross-link many chains into a network and rubber's stress-strain curve appears beside Hooke's law, with the warming on stretching shown on a thermometer.
takeaway: Rubber pulls back not because its bonds are stretched but because a stretched chain has fewer shapes to be in, so it pulls harder when hotter and warms when stretched, the opposite of a metal spring.
pitfall: The force in rubber is entropic, not from stretched bonds: a rubber band heated under a weight contracts, which a steel spring never does.
why: MIT OCW 3.064 Polymer Engineering lecture on chain conformation and the kinetic theory of rubber elasticity (and Feynman's much-shared rubber-band clip): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-064-polymer-engineering-fall-2003/resources/lec_6

title: Substitution mechanisms: SN1 and SN2
interaction: Step a nucleophile toward a carbon bearing a leaving group across an energy surface built from two coupled bond curves (an empirical valence-bond model) plus an ionic state whose energy drops as the solvent-polarity slider rises: the surface shows either a single pass with the nucleophile arriving from the back or a two-step route through a flat carbocation. Keep it in the dark and it still sprouts, pale and tall, while the food packed inside it shrinks; its weight falls until the leaves open and only then starts to climb.
takeaway: A seed needs water and warmth to wake up, not light or soil: it lives off the food packed inside it until its own leaves open.
needsSource: none: the hydrothermal-time germination model (Gummerson 1986; Bradford 2002) has no light term; the seedling's mass falls on its reserves and rises once leaves open; bean parameters stated on the page
pitfall: Seeds are not dead and do not need soil; and the seedling gets lighter, not heavier, until it can make its own food. Light matters for growing, not for sprouting.
why: NGSS 5-LS1-1, taught with bean seeds sprouting on a wet paper towel in a bag with no soil. https://thewonderofscience.com/5ls11
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page starts once there is a leaf in the light; this one is everything before the first leaf opens.

title: Tree rings
interaction: Scrub the years of a real tree's life and watch it lay down one ring a year, wide in a good year and narrow in a dry one, drawn to the measured widths from a public archive; hover a ring for its year and its measured width, and the narrow ones are the hard years. Then try the detectives' trick: slide the ring pattern of an old beam along a living tree's record until the narrow years line up, and read off when the beam was cut.
takeaway: A tree writes one ring a year, wide in good years and narrow in bad ones, so its rings are both a calendar and a weather diary that can be matched between trees.
needs: Raw ring-width series (.rwl) from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank, NOAA NCEI World Data Service for Paleoclimatology: a US government archive, catalogued as CC0 by the Open Data Institute; each contributed series cites its authors.
needsSource: ITRDB ring-width series, NOAA NCEI (US government archive, CC0 per the ODI certificate; data.gov lists no licence, so confirm on the study page)
pitfall: Not every ring is a year everywhere: in a bad year a tree can skip a ring or add a false one, which is why the match uses a whole pattern of narrow years, never a single count.
why: Demand and data: the ITRDB is the world's largest public archive of tree-ring measurements, catalogued on data.gov. https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/noaa-wds-paleoclimatology-the-international-tree-ring-data-bank-itrdb-revisited
overlapWith: deep-time: that page scrubs Earth's whole record; this one scrubs one tree's rings, one per year, and teaches the matching trick that dates old wood.

title: Why big birds flap slowly
interaction: Pick a real bird, from a hummingbird to a swan, and see it flap at its own rate and fly at the speed it needs to stay up; drag the size slider to blow a sparrow up to goose size and watch the flap rate fall and the needed speed climb. Past a certain size the sums no longer work for flapping, and the biggest flyers are shown soaring instead.
takeaway: Bigger birds must fly faster and flap slower, and past a certain size flapping cannot keep them up, which is why the biggest flyers soar.
needs: AVONET (Tobias et al. 2022, Ecology Letters, paper CC BY 4.0; the data files on Figshare, licence to confirm) for species mass, wing length and wing area; Pennycuick's wingbeat-frequency formula (J. Exp. Biol. 1990, revised 1996) and minimum flight speed from wing loading.
needsSource: AVONET species measurements (paper CC BY 4.0, dataset licence to confirm on the repository); Pennycuick 1990/1996 published formulas
pitfall: Do not explain lift here: flight owns it, and never with equal transit time. A bird's size does not scale evenly: weight grows faster than wing area, which is the whole point.
why: Demand: the universal flapping-frequency equation made popular-science news in 2024. https://physicsworld.com/a/simple-equation-predicts-how-quickly-animals-flap-their-wings/
overlapWith: flight: that page is lift and stall on a wing section at level 2; this one never looks at the wing's shape, only at how flap rate and speed change with a bird's size across real species.

title: Why leaves change colour
interaction: Watch one maple leaf from late summer into autumn on a calendar scrub: as the days shorten and the nights cool, the green pigment is broken down and pulled back into the tree, and the yellow and orange that were underneath all along show through; sunny days with cold nights brew red on top. Then force the weather: a warm, dull autumn gives yellow without red, and an early frost cuts the show short.
takeaway: The yellow was in the leaf all summer, hidden under the green; the tree takes the green back before letting the leaf go.
needsSource: none for the model (green pigment broken down as days shorten and cool, yellow pigments constant, red made on bright cool days, leaf colour mixed from the pigments); if the colour is mixed from measured pigment spectra, PhotochemCAD's spectra are freely downloadable but their licence must be checked
pitfall: Leaves do not make yellow in autumn: the yellow was already there, and only the red is made fresh. Cold does not cause the change by itself: the shortening days are the main trigger.
why: England KS1 statutory requirement, Seasonal changes: observe changes across the four seasons; and the most-asked autumn question. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page is the green pigment at work; this one is the green being dismantled and what it leaves behind.

title: Bacterial chemotaxis
interaction: Release a few hundred E. coli into a dish with a drop of attractant and watch each one run straight, tumble, and run again; inside each cell a Barkai-Leibler receptor model sets the tumble rate, and the swarm drifts up the gradient. Move the drop, flood the dish with a uniform dose and watch the tumble rate dip then recover exactly (perfect adaptation), and change the adaptation time or the swim speed to see the biased random walk fail.
takeaway: A bacterium is too small to sense a gradient across its body, so it compares now with a moment ago and tumbles less when things are getting better; that biased random walk is enough to climb a gradient.
pitfall: The cell does not steer toward the attractant: it cannot tell direction, it only changes how often it tumbles, and the page must not draw it turning toward the source.
why: CourseSource lesson on building and simulating a chemotaxis model in Cell Collective (QUBES): https://qubeshub.org/publications/5179/
overlapWith: ecosystems: that page moves animals on a field by population rates; here each cell's movement follows an internal signalling model and the collective drift emerges from it.
needsSource: none

title: Cell cycle control
interaction: Run the Novak-Tyson model of the cyclin-Cdk switch: cyclin accumulates, Cdk activity stays low until a threshold, then flips high through its positive feedback loops and the cell enters mitosis; the negative loop through the anaphase-promoting complex destroys cyclin and resets it. Raise and lower cyclin by hand to trace the hysteresis loop, change the cell's growth rate to see the period change, and apply a DNA-damage checkpoint that holds the switch off.
takeaway: A cell divides when a bistable switch flips, not when a timer runs out: positive feedback makes the decision sharp and hard to reverse, and checkpoints work by holding the switch below its threshold.
needs: Tyson 1991 cyclin-Cdc2 model (BioModels BIOMD0000000005, CC0) or the Novak-Tyson 1993 model as curated in BioModels (CC0).
pitfall: The cycle is not a clock that ticks regardless of state; in the model it is a relaxation oscillator built on a bistable switch, and the page must show the switch flipping, not a smooth sine wave.
why: Tyson & Novak, 'Cell Cycle Vignettes: Bistability and Oscillations' (Virginia Tech teaching note): https://www.biol.vt.edu/content/dam/biol_vt_edu/faculty/tyson/Bistability%20and%20Oscillations.pdf
overlapWith: cancer: that page lets cells divide too often by mutation; this one shows the machinery that decides when a single cell divides, which cancer's mutations break.
needsSource: BioModels curated models, CC0.

title: Central pattern generators
interaction: Connect two neuron models with mutual inhibition and give them a steady, unpatterned drive; they fall into alternating bursts, the half-centre oscillator. Change the drive to speed the rhythm, swap the burst-ending mechanism (adaptation versus post-inhibitory rebound), then chain twenty such pairs along a lamprey's spine with asymmetric coupling: a wave of contraction travels down the body and the fish swims; reverse the coupling bias and it swims backward.
takeaway: Rhythmic movement does not need a rhythmic command: two cells that inhibit each other turn a constant signal into alternation, and a chain of them makes a travelling wave.
pitfall: The half-centre model is a model: lamprey experiments show left-right phasing can survive midline lesions, so the page must present it as the classic mechanism, not the settled one.
why: Model repository rather than a syllabus: lamprey swimming CPG reference implementation in the Nengo model zoo, https://zoo.nengo.ai/submissions/lamprey/index.html (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: neurons: that page fires one neuron and sums inputs on the next; this one wires neurons into a circuit whose output is a rhythm none of them has alone.
needsSource: none

title: Circadian clocks
interaction: Run a clock gene that represses its own transcription through a delay (a Goodwin-type loop, with the Leloup-Goldbeter model for the real gene names) and watch mRNA and protein chase each other in a cycle close to 24 hours in constant darkness. Add a light input to the degradation term and the clock locks to the day; shift the light schedule by eight hours and count how many days the phase takes to catch up, eastward versus westward; shorten the delay and the rhythm stops.
takeaway: A gene that switches itself off with a delay oscillates on its own, and daylight does not drive that rhythm but nudges it into step, which is why jet lag takes days to resolve.
needs: Leloup & Goldbeter circadian model as curated in BioModels (CC0); the Goodwin oscillator needs no data.
pitfall: The rhythm persists without any external cue: the page must show free-running oscillation in constant darkness, and must not show the clock as a response to sunrise.
why: MPI MiS course on mathematical modelling of circadian rhythms: https://www.mis.mpg.de/events/event/mathematical-modeling-of-circadian-rhythms
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page is a mass on a spring driven by a force; this is a limit-cycle oscillator made of a delayed negative feedback loop, entrained rather than driven.
needsSource: BioModels curated models, CC0.

title: The coalescent
interaction: Sample ten gene copies from a population and step backwards one generation at a time: each copy picks a parent at random, two lineages that pick the same parent merge, and the genealogy grows down to a single ancestor with its branch lengths. Rerun to see how much the tree varies, change the population size and watch the time to the common ancestor scale with it, and sprinkle mutations on the branches to produce the sample's sequence differences. Squeeze the population through a bottleneck and see the genealogy and the diversity collapse.
takeaway: The pattern of differences in a sample of DNA sequences is the shadow of a random genealogy, and reading that genealogy backwards tells you how large the population was and when it shrank.
pitfall: The most recent common ancestor of a sample is not the first human or a single couple; different genes have different ancestors at different times, and the page should show two loci with different trees.
why: coalesceR, a pedagogical R package for teaching the basics of coalescent theory: https://rdrr.io/rforge/coalesceR
overlapWith: population-genetics: that page runs time forward for a whole population; this one runs it backward for a sample, which is how real sequence data are read.
needsSource: none

title: DNA sequencing & genome assembly
interaction: Sequence a real virus: run a Sanger reaction and sort its fluorescent fragments by length into a chromatogram, then switch to shotgun reads of the whole phiX174 genome and assemble them yourself. Choose read length, coverage and k, watch the de Bruijn graph form from k-mers and collapse into contigs, see repeats tangle the graph and sequencing errors sprout dead ends, and compare the assembly with the true genome.
takeaway: A genome is never read in one piece: it is read as many short overlapping fragments and recovered by a graph algorithm whose success depends on coverage, read length and the genome's repeats.
needs: The phiX174 genome (GenBank NC_001422, 5,386 bases; NCBI places no restrictions on reuse of GenBank records).
pitfall: Sequencing does not read a chromosome end to end; the page must show that short reads lose information in repeats longer than a read, which no amount of coverage recovers.
why: NUS CS4330 lecture 'Practical de Bruijn graph assembly' (a standard bioinformatics-course exercise is assembling phiX174): https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~wongls/courses/cs4330/2024/12-practical-dbg-assembly.pdf
overlapWith: crispr: that page cuts DNA at a matched site; this one reads DNA, and its algorithmic core (graphs of overlapping k-mers) has no counterpart in the catalogue.
needsSource: GenBank NC_001422, no reuse restrictions (NCBI policy).

title: Epigenetic memory
interaction: Run a row of nucleosomes that carry a silencing or an activating mark; each marked nucleosome recruits enzymes that convert others, including non-neighbours, and every cell division dilutes the marks by half. Set the recruitment strength and feedback range and watch the row lock into all-silent or all-active and hold that state through dozens of divisions; weaken the cooperativity and the memory decays; force the region silent with a transient pulse and see the state persist after the pulse is gone.
takeaway: A cell can remember a decision without changing its DNA: marks on chromatin that recruit their own copiers form a bistable system that survives being halved at each division.
pitfall: Most chromatin marks are reset between generations; the page must not slide from cellular memory into inheritance of acquired characteristics across organisms.
why: Lecture video rather than a syllabus: math-institute lecture on the Dodd-Sneppen nucleosome-modification model of epigenetic memory, https://mathinstitutes.org/videos/4418 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page reads a gene; this one decides whether the gene stays readable at all, through marks on the packaging rather than the sequence (model of Dodd et al. 2007).
needsSource: none

title: Evolutionary game theory
interaction: Set the payoffs of a hawk-dove contest and release a population of players; replicator dynamics pulls the share of hawks to the mixed equilibrium that neither strategy can invade, drawn as a flow on a line. Switch to the prisoner's dilemma and watch cooperators die out, then place the players on a grid where they meet neighbours and see clusters of cooperators survive; add relatedness between players and find the cost-to-benefit ratio at which helping kin pays, Hamilton's rule.
takeaway: When fitness depends on what others do, the winning strategy is the one that cannot be invaded rather than the one that scores most, and cooperation survives only when cooperators meet each other more often than chance.
pitfall: Evolutionary stability does not mean the population is at its best: hawks persist even though a population of doves would score higher, and the page must show that the equilibrium is not the optimum.
why: ELTE course on evolutionary game theory (hawk-dove, replicator dynamics, ESS, altruism): https://neptun.elte.hu/MobilityCourses/Course/evojatsb22em
overlapWith: evolution: that page's fitness is fixed by the environment; here fitness depends on what the rest of the population does, which produces equilibria that selection on a fixed landscape never does. It also covers the biological half of the Reserve item 'Game theory' (replicator dynamics, ESS), leaving classical game theory to a math lens.
needsSource: none

title: Noise in gene expression
interaction: Run a single gene with the Gillespie algorithm: the promoter flicks on and off, each on-period fires a burst of mRNAs, each mRNA a burst of proteins. Set the switching, transcription, translation and decay rates and watch the protein count jitter in one cell while a histogram across a thousand cells widens or narrows. Add a second identical reporter to the same cell and plot one against the other: scatter along the diagonal is shared, extrinsic noise; scatter across it is the gene's own, intrinsic noise.
takeaway: Genetically identical cells in the same environment differ because their molecules are counted in tens and made in bursts, and a two-reporter scatter plot separates the randomness of the gene itself from the randomness of the cell around it.
pitfall: Noise does not simply average out at higher expression: bursty expression keeps the Fano factor above one, so the model must produce bursts, not a Poisson stream of single proteins.
why: LMU Munich 'Biophysics of Systems' lecture on stochastic gene expression (Elowitz 2002 two-reporter experiment): https://www2.physik.uni-muenchen.de/lehre/vorlesungen/wise_20_21/Biophysics_of_Systems/04b_StochasticGenes_2E.pdf
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: that page shows averages converging; here the counts are so small that the fluctuations are the biology, and bursts keep them from averaging out.
needsSource: none

title: Synthetic gene circuits: toggle switch & repressilator
interaction: Wire promoters, repressors and a fluorescent reporter into a circuit on a plasmid, set repression strength, cooperativity and degradation rates, and run it. Two genes that repress each other make a switch that a pulse of inducer flips and that stays flipped; three in a ring make an oscillator whose fluorescence blinks, and the reader finds the parameter region where the blinking dies. A stochastic solver shows the same circuit jitter in a single cell.
takeaway: Two genes that repress each other remember a state and three in a ring keep time, so the logic of a cell's control can be built from a handful of parts, and whether a circuit works depends on the numbers, not just the wiring.
needs: Repressilator model of Elowitz & Leibler 2000 as curated in BioModels (BIOMD0000000012, CC0); toggle-switch equations and parameters from Gardner, Cantor & Collins 2000 (published values, no dataset).
pitfall: Oscillation is not guaranteed by the ring: with weak repression or low cooperativity the repressilator settles to a steady state, so the page must show the dead region rather than a circuit that always blinks.
why: Yale 'Biologic' module teaching the toggle switch and repressilator to biology and premedical students: https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3126
overlapWith: logic-gates: that page composes ideal digital gates; here each gate is a leaky, continuous repressor with a time constant, and the question is which wirings still switch or oscillate.
needsSource: BioModels curated repressilator (CC0); toggle-switch parameters from the paper, no dataset needed.

title: The genetic code's error tolerance
interaction: Hover any codon in the genetic-code table to see which amino acids one base change can reach, coloured by how different their chemistry is, and total a cost for the whole code. Then press shuffle: the page draws thousands of random codes that keep the same block structure, scores each one, and builds a histogram with the standard code marked; change the cost measure (polarity, volume, charge) or the mutation bias and watch where the standard code lands.
takeaway: Most single-base errors in the real code swap an amino acid for a chemically similar one, and among random codes with the same structure only a tiny fraction do better, though how tiny depends on what you measure.
needs: Amino-acid polar requirement (Woese 1966) and other physico-chemical scales from the published literature; the standard code table (public domain).
pitfall: The 'one in a million' figure holds only for polar requirement with a transition/transversion bias; with volume or charge the standard code is far less special, and the page must not present the code as uniquely optimal.
why: Freeland & Hurst 1998 as a course reading in Swarthmore Phys 120: https://www.sccs.swarthmore.edu/users/08/bblonder/phys120/docs/freeland.pdf
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page shows what one mutation does to one protein; this one scores the whole table against every alternative code.
needsSource: Published amino-acid property scales (literature values); code table public domain.

title: Gene regulation & the lac operon
interaction: Set the lactose and glucose in a bacterium's medium and watch an ODE model of the lac operon respond: the repressor leaves the operator when an inducer is present, CAP recruits the polymerase only when glucose is low, and the permease the operon makes imports more inducer. Sweep the inducer up and then down to trace the hysteresis loop, and grow a culture on both sugars to see the diauxic pause when the glucose runs out.
takeaway: A bacterium switches a set of genes on only when their product is useful and nothing better is around, and positive feedback through its own transporter turns that switch into a memory: the same inducer level can leave the operon on or off depending on where it came from.
pitfall: Bistability and hysteresis were measured with the gratuitous inducer TMG; with plain lactose the loop is weak or absent because lactose is also consumed, so the page must not present lactose itself as a memory switch.
why: MIT OCW 7.01SC Fundamentals of Biology, module 'Gene Regulation and the Lac Operon': https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/7-01sc-fundamentals-of-biology-fall-2011/resources/molecbio_sess5
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page reads one gene into a protein; this one is about when the gene is read at all, as a dynamical switch with feedback (model of Ozbudak et al. 2004).
needsSource: none

title: Luria-Delbruck: mutations before selection
interaction: Step through the 1943 experiment: grow twenty cultures from single cells for a chosen number of generations at a chosen mutation rate, plate them all on a phage lawn, and count the survivors. If mutations arose only on contact with the phage the counts would be Poisson and nearly equal; instead a few plates hold hundreds of mutants, the jackpots, because a mutation that happened early was inherited by a whole clone. Replay with mutations induced at plating to see the Poisson alternative, and estimate the mutation rate from the fraction of empty plates.
takeaway: Mutations happen before and regardless of the challenge they will later face, and the wild spread between replicate cultures is the signature of that.
pitfall: The jackpot distribution does not show that the environment induces mutations; it shows the opposite, and the page must make the Poisson alternative explicit so the reader sees it fail.
why: 'Fascination with Fluctuation: Luria and Delbruck's Legacy', on the experiment in undergraduate mathematics education (University of Delaware): https://udspace.udel.edu/items/2837763f-b87a-465a-9701-2b96405d98f5/full
overlapWith: evolution: that page's pitfall says mutations do not arise because they are needed; this one is the experiment that proved it, run as a statistics-of-clones simulation.
needsSource: none

title: Membrane transport & the resting potential
interaction: Drag the ion concentrations on each side of a membrane and the permeability of each channel type, and watch ions cross while the voltage settles: with only potassium channels open it sits at the Nernst potential, and as sodium leaks in it drifts toward the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz value shown live. Switch the sodium-potassium pump off and watch the gradients, the voltage and the cell's volume decay over simulated hours; then dilute the outside solution and see water follow the ions.
takeaway: A cell's voltage is a weighted average of each ion's equilibrium potential, weighted by how permeable the membrane is to it, and holding that voltage and the cell's volume costs a steady stream of ATP through the pump.
